title: Scale-Invariant Lifelong Cross-Modal Hashing via Gradient Equilibrium

problem.claim: Real-world multimedia streams have severely imbalanced task scales, creating challenges for lifelong cross-modal hashing.

gap.claim: Existing lifelong cross-modal hashing methods implicitly assume balanced task sizes and do not account for gradient submergence under imbalance.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes Scale-Invariant Lifelong Cross-Modal Hashing, a framework designed to achieve gradient equilibrium regardless of task-size ratios.
The paper derives inverse-scale normalization weights and provides an exact scale-invariance result, including analysis of smoothing's stabilizing role.
The paper reports reduced catastrophic forgetting, improved MAP under extreme imbalance, and linear training complexity.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on MIRFlickr, NUS-WIDE, and MS-COCO reportedly reduce catastrophic forgetting by 70% compared with state-of-the-art methods.
Under a 10:1 task-size ratio, the method reportedly achieves up to 3.7% MAP improvement while maintaining linear training complexity.

narrative_sequence.summary: Multimedia streams exhibit severe task-scale imbalance.
Existing methods assume balanced task sizes, while gradient submergence can cause forgetting or poor plasticity.
SILCH uses scale-invariant gradient equilibrium and inverse-scale normalization to address arbitrary task-size imbalance.
The analysis establishes scale invariance for the weights and explains smoothing's stabilizing role.
Experiments report improvements in forgetting and MAP under imbalance with linear training complexity.

source_observation.claim: Inverse-scale normalization is reported to make old and new tasks contribute comparable gradients under arbitrary task-size imbalance.

interpretation.claim: Balancing optimization influence by task scale may help manage the plasticity-stability trade-off in lifelong learning.

application.claim: For sequential learning systems exposed to uneven task volumes, consider normalization schemes that compensate for task-scale differences.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether inverse-scale balancing is appropriate when task sizes are not the main source of gradient imbalance.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the experimental protocols, baseline identities, or statistical variation behind the reported results.
The abstract does not describe the model architecture, optimization procedure, or smoothing implementation in detail.
The abstract does not provide full conditions for the theoretical result or define the scope of arbitrary imbalance beyond the stated examples.
